mean: but; used to add a point that goes against what came before
ex: The flat in Andheri is close to the station. However, the rent is far above our budget.
note: At sentence start, put a comma after it: 'However, ...'. To join two clauses use a semicolon: 'It rained; however, play continued.' A comma alone is wrong.
ex2: Rohit was out in the first over. However, the middle order held firm and India won with two balls to spare.

mean: even though; admits one fact before a contrasting one
ex: Although the train was three hours late, Deepa still reached Bhopal in time for the mehendi.
note: Never 'although ... but': 'Although it rained, but we played' is wrong. Use one: 'Although it rained, we played.' Comma after the although-clause when it comes first.
ex2: Although Ammachi in Kottayam has a smartphone, she still prefers a landline call from her grandchildren every Sunday.

mean: for that reason; as a result
ex: The exam centre is in Thane and the locals are packed; therefore, Aman left home at six.
note: A formal 'so'. Joining two clauses, put a semicolon or full stop before it and a comma after: 'It rained; therefore, we stayed.'
ex2: The doctor found Ayesha's iron levels low; therefore, she was told to eat more spinach, dates and jaggery.

mean: in place of something else; as the other choice
ex: The canteen ran out of dosa, so Siddharth had idli instead.
note: 'Instead of' + noun or -ing: 'instead of going', never 'instead of to go'. At sentence start: 'Instead, ...' with a comma.
ex2: Gaurav didn't post an angry reply in the family WhatsApp group; he called his uncle instead.

mean: except if; if not
ex: Unless you renew your driving licence before Monday, the RTO will charge a late fee.
note: Unless already means 'if not', so don't add another 'not'. Use present tense for the future: 'unless it rains', not 'unless it will rain'.
ex2: Unless the rain stops by four, the match at Chinnaswamy Stadium will be called off.

mean: while on the other hand; compares two different facts
ex: Chennai gets most of its rain from October to December, whereas Mumbai gets it from June to September.
note: Joins two contrasting facts inside one sentence, usually with a comma before it. Don't start a standalone sentence with it the way you would with 'However,'.
ex2: Arjun saves every rupee of his stipend, whereas his twin sister Anjali spends hers on concerts and street food.

mean: also, and more importantly; adds a stronger point
ex: The new route saves twenty minutes. Moreover, it avoids the underpass near Sion that floods every July.
note: Starts a sentence, or follows a semicolon, with a comma after: 'Moreover, ...'. A comma alone before it is wrong. In speech, 'what's more' is lighter.
ex2: The candidate could not answer basic Excel questions. Moreover, she arrived forty minutes late for the interview in Gurugram.

mean: even though something happened; without being stopped by it
ex: Despite the heavy rain, the Durga Puja pandal in Salt Lake was packed till midnight.
note: Never 'despite of'. Use 'despite + noun/-ing' or 'in spite of'. Before a full clause write 'despite the fact that'. Comma after a leading despite-phrase.
ex2: Despite her fever, Lalitha sat the board exam and still scored ninety-two in maths.

mean: even so; in spite of what was just said
ex: The team was missing two senior players; nevertheless, they won the Ranji match by an innings.
note: One word, not 'never the less'. After a full stop or semicolon, with a comma after it. A little stronger and more formal than 'however'.
ex2: The station chai was far too sweet; nevertheless, Imran drank two cups to stay awake on the night train.

mean: at the same time, while something else is happening
ex: Papa went to queue at the ration shop; meanwhile, Mummy put the rajma on to soak.
note: Usually at sentence start with a comma: 'Meanwhile, ...'. 'In the meantime' means the same. News uses it to switch scenes: 'Meanwhile, in Guwahati...'
ex2: The elders were busy with the pheras; meanwhile, the children quietly finished off the gulab jamuns.

mean: if not; if that does not happen, then
ex: Carry an umbrella to the interview; otherwise, you'll reach the Bandra office soaking wet.
note: Joining two clauses needs a semicolon or full stop before it: '...; otherwise, ...'. A comma alone is a common error. 'Or else' is the casual version.
ex2: Save your file every few minutes; otherwise, one power cut in Patna can wipe out the whole assignment.

mean: in addition; also, as one more reason
ex: I'd rather skip the reception; besides, I have an early flight to Kochi tomorrow.
note: 'Besides' (with s) = in addition. 'Beside' (no s) = next to: 'sit beside me'. As a connector: 'Besides, ...' with a comma.
ex2: We can't buy a car this year; besides, there is no parking space in our narrow Lajpat Nagar lane.

mean: as a result of what has just been said
ex: The portal was down all morning; consequently, hundreds of students missed the scholarship deadline.
note: Like 'therefore': full stop or semicolon before it, comma after. Don't confuse with 'subsequently', which only means 'later', not 'as a result'.
ex2: Thick fog covered north India; consequently, dozens of flights out of Delhi were delayed till noon.

mean: in the same way; also
ex: Mehul thanked the volunteers at the gurdwara langar, and the visiting students did likewise.
note: At sentence start: 'Likewise, ...' with a comma. 'Do likewise' = do the same. Replying 'Likewise' to 'Nice to meet you' is fine.
ex2: Our Kolkata branch cut its paper use by half, and the Pune office now plans to do likewise.

mean: only if; on the condition that
ex: You can borrow my scooter for the weekend, provided that you fill the tank before returning it.
note: Stronger than 'if': it sets a condition. 'That' can be dropped ('provided you pay'). Use present tense after it, not 'will'. Comma before it.
ex2: The panchayat will repair the village road before the monsoon, provided that the district funds arrive on time.

mean: used to show that two things are very different
ex: Rajasthan's summers are dry and scorching; in contrast, Meghalaya stays cool and wet most of the year.
note: 'In contrast, ...' starts a sentence with a comma; 'in contrast to X' compares inside one sentence. Noun is KON-trast; the verb is kun-TRAST.
ex2: Most of the hostel slept through Sunday morning; in contrast, Kiran was at the library by seven.

mean: also; adds another point to an argument
ex: The new hostel has no night warden. Furthermore, the main gate lock has been broken for weeks.
note: Sentence start, comma after. Moreover and furthermore are near twins; never stack them ('Moreover, furthermore'). Plain 'also' often reads better.
ex2: The startup's sales are growing fast in Jaipur. Furthermore, two large investors have shown interest.

mean: for this reason; also, from now
ex: The monsoon was weak this year, hence the jump in vegetable prices at Azadpur mandi.
note: Often takes just a noun, no verb: 'hence the delay'. 'From hence' is wrong; 'hence' already includes 'from'. In casual writing, 'so' is simpler.
ex2: Ritika had a night shift at the hospital, hence her absence from the family lunch.

mean: although; used before a short phrase, not a full clause
ex: The metro extension finally opened, albeit two years late and well over budget.
note: Goes after a comma, before a short phrase: 'a win, albeit narrow'. Never add a subject and verb: not 'albeit it was narrow'. Say awl-BEE-it.
ex2: Dadaji agreed to try a video call, albeit with plenty of grumbling about the tiny screen.

mean: in spite of; without being stopped by
ex: Notwithstanding the heavy rain, lakhs of warkaris walked on towards Pandharpur for Ashadhi Ekadashi.
note: Very formal, common in contracts and court orders. Can come before or after the noun: 'these problems notwithstanding'. In normal writing, 'despite' is better.
ex2: Notwithstanding his sore shoulder, the young bowler from Bihar finished his full ten overs.

mean: by doing this; as a result of that action
ex: The farmer switched to drip irrigation, thereby cutting his water use almost by half.
note: After a comma, followed by an -ing verb: ', thereby saving time'. It links an action to its result. Not the same as 'thereafter' (after that).
ex2: The school added eggs to the mid-day meal, thereby raising attendance across the whole block.

mean: by which; through which a system or plan works
ex: The housing society set up a system whereby residents pay maintenance by UPI and get an instant receipt.
note: Comes right after a noun like system, scheme or rule, with no comma. Formal. Don't mix it up with 'whereas' (contrast) or 'thereby' (result).
ex2: The company brought in a policy whereby staff can work from home every Friday.

mean: to the extent that; only as far as
ex: The new rule helps, insofar as it gives night-shift staff a safe cab home.
note: It limits a claim: true only to that degree. Write 'insofar as' (British also 'in so far as'), never 'insofar that'. Usually a comma before it.
ex2: The new diet helped Rakesh insofar as he slept better, but his weight stayed the same.

mean: in the opposite way; looking at it the other way round
ex: When the rupee falls, imports cost more; conversely, textile exporters in Tiruppur earn more.
note: Use it for a reversal of the same relationship, not for any difference ('in contrast' fits that). Semicolon or full stop before it, comma after.
ex2: A good monsoon cheers farmers in Vidarbha; conversely, a weak one can leave them deep in debt.

mean: until now; up to this time
ex: The Keezhadi excavation revealed a hitherto unknown picture of early city life in Tamil Nadu.
note: Formal and old-fashioned; today it mostly sits before an adjective ('hitherto unknown'), not at sentence start. In speech, say 'until now' or 'so far'.
ex2: The new bridge links villages that were hitherto cut off for weeks every monsoon.

mean: in relation to; compared with
ex: The finance head asked how our costs looked vis-à-vis last year before approving the Diwali bonus.
note: French: the final s is silent, veez-ah-VEE. Indian office letters overuse it; 'regarding' or 'compared with' usually reads better. Goes before a noun, no comma.
ex2: At the RWA meeting, Mr D'Souza asked where the committee stood vis-à-vis the new parking rules.

mean: because of this; so this happened next
ex: Heavy rain flooded the tracks at Kurla. As a result, local trains ran forty minutes late.
note: 'As a result' starts a new sentence or follows a semicolon. 'As a result of' takes a noun: 'as a result of the strike'.
ex2: Sunita practised her speech every evening; as a result, she spoke without notes at the school assembly.

mean: also; used to add one more point
ex: The job pays well. In addition, the company gives free lunch and a cab home after nine.
note: Comma after 'In addition' at the start. 'In addition to' takes a noun or -ing form: 'in addition to cooking', not 'in addition to cook'.
ex2: In addition to her college classes, Fatima teaches tailoring to women in her Bhopal mohalla.

mean: only if; on the condition that
ex: You can play cricket in the lane as long as you finish your homework first.
note: Use the present tense after it, even for the future: 'as long as you finish', not 'as long as you will finish'.
ex2: The landlord in Koramangala said pets are fine as long as they don't scratch the floors.

mean: used to give the opposite side of a point
ex: A flat in Thane is cheaper. On the other hand, the daily commute to Churchgate takes two hours.
with: on the one hand ... on the other hand
note: Often paired with 'on the one hand'. Use it to weigh two sides of one choice, not simply to add a point.
ex2: Ishita loves the buzz of Delhi; her brother, on the other hand, misses the quiet of their Dehradun home.

mean: as a safety step, because something might happen
ex: Take a jacket in case it gets cold on the overnight bus to Manali.
note: 'In case' means a precaution taken now: 'Take an umbrella in case it rains.' It is not the same as 'if'. Avoid 'if suppose'.
ex2: Kabir saved his hall ticket on his phone in case the printout got wet in the rain.

mean: instead of; choosing one thing and not the other
ex: Rather than argue on the family WhatsApp group, Joseph called his cousin and talked it out.
note: Keep both sides in the same form: 'walk rather than drive', 'by train rather than by bus'.
ex2: The panchayat chose to repair the old village well rather than dig yet another borewell.

mean: but in spite of that
ex: The pitch was wet and slow. Even so, the Hyderabad openers scored sixty in the powerplay.
note: Comes at the start of a sentence or after a semicolon, with a comma after it. Like 'nevertheless', but less formal.
ex2: Flights to Kochi cost a fortune in December; even so, the Menons booked six tickets for the wedding.

mean: because of the fact that; keeping this in mind
ex: Given that the exam is on Monday, Ananya decided to skip her cousin's sangeet on Sunday.
note: 'Given that' + a clause; 'given' + a noun: 'given the traffic'. Both mean 'considering'.
ex2: The village school did remarkably well, given that it had only two teachers for five classes.

mean: because of; after thinking about some new fact
ex: In light of the heavy rain warning, all schools in Chennai will stay shut tomorrow.
note: Both 'in light of' and 'in the light of' are correct; British usage often prefers 'in the light of'. Fairly formal.
ex2: In light of her strong work, the Indore firm offered Pooja a full-time job before her internship ended.

mean: used to say that the opposite is true
ex: The new coach is not harsh. On the contrary, the boys say he is the most patient one they have had.
note: Use it to reject a statement and say the opposite. To compare two different things, use 'on the other hand' or 'in contrast'.
ex2: Moving back to the village was no step backwards for Harpreet; on the contrary, her dairy business is booming.

mean: so; in a way that suits what was just said
ex: Our flight to Guwahati was three hours late, and the hotel changed our check-in time accordingly.
note: Many Indians say 'as per that'. 'Accordingly' is cleaner: 'We will plan accordingly.' At the start of a sentence, put a comma after it.
ex2: The forecast warned of heavy rain; accordingly, the organisers moved the garba night indoors.

mean: for the same reason; the same idea applies here too
ex: If we cheer players when they win, by the same token we should stand by them when they lose.
note: It shows that the same reasoning applies to a second case. Common in debates and editorials.
ex2: Parents want children to keep phones away at dinner; by the same token, they should do the same.

mean: in order to reach that goal
ex: The district wants every child in school by June; to that end, teachers are visiting each house.
note: It points back to a goal just mentioned. 'To this end' means the same. Don't confuse it with 'at the end'.
ex2: Sameer wants to run the Mumbai Marathon. To that end, he jogs along Marine Drive every morning.

mean: in place of; instead of
ex: Staff who work on Diwali get a day off in lieu of the holiday.
with: a day off in lieu of
note: Say 'loo', not 'lee-yoo'. Common in office and legal writing: 'a month's salary in lieu of notice'.
ex2: The shopkeeper gave Revathi two toffees in lieu of the two rupees change.

mean: even so; that may be true, but
ex: You may have had a long day; be that as it may, the guests arrive at eight and the biryani isn't ready.
with: but be that as it may
note: It accepts a point without arguing about it, then moves on. Formal; natural in debates and essays, odd in casual chat.
ex2: The flyover may ease traffic in ten years. Be that as it may, the commute to Hinjewadi is terrible right now.

mean: so that something bad does not happen; for fear that
ex: Mohan whispered in the reading room lest the strict librarian throw him out.
note: Formal. After 'lest' use the base verb or 'should': 'lest he forget' or 'lest he should forget', never 'lest he doesn't'.
ex2: The editor checked every figure twice, lest the newspaper be accused of printing a false story.
